issues.legal_issue: A defective or deliberately improper investigation does not by itself require acquittal when the prosecution evidence, independently assessed, is reliable and proves the case.
material_facts: Two injured eyewitnesses and another eyewitness gave consistent accounts of the assault, and the Court found their presence and testimony reliable.

The investigating officer did not account for the deceased’s viscera or establish whether it had been sent for forensic examination, and failed to record the doctor’s explanation for the absence of injuries in the post-mortem report.

The investigation and medical evidence contained serious omissions and contradictions, but other evidence, including the eyewitness accounts and contemporaneous investigative records, supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The investigation was deliberately and seriously defective, but that defect did not entitle the accused to acquittal because the reliable prosecution evidence independently established guilt.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sathi Prasad v. State of U.P. (1972) 3 SCC 613, Dhanaj Singh v. State of Punjab (2004) 3 SCC 654, Paras Yadav v. State of Bihar, AIR 1999 SC 644, State of Karnataka v. K. Yarappa Reddy, 2000 SCC (Cri) 61, Karnel Singh v. State of M.P. (1995) 5 SCC 518, and Ram Bali v. State of U.P. (2004) 10 SCC 598, courts must scrutinize the evidence independently and carefully when investigation is defective; they must not acquit solely because of that defect, particularly where doing so would reward a designedly defective investigation. The Court also relied on C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 2010 SC 3718, concerning the effect of investigative defects.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and investigation_defective and eyewitnesses_credible and corroborating_evidence_supports_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.investigation_defective: The investigation contains significant omissions, commissions, or other defects.
predicates.eyewitnesses_credible: The court finds the eyewitnesses’ presence and accounts reliable.
predicates.corroborating_evidence_supports_account: Other evidence supports the reliable eyewitness account.

issues.definition: When a conviction appeal involves a defective investigation but credible eyewitnesses and supporting evidence, the defect alone does not result in setting aside the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Credible eyewitness testimony may be accepted despite conflicting medical evidence when the medical opinion does not conclusively exclude the account and is unreliable or inadequately reasoned.
material_facts: The post-mortem report recorded no external or internal injuries and did not determine the cause of death.
The eyewitnesses consistently described a fatal assault, and the investigating officer and persons present at the inquest recorded injuries on the deceased’s body.
The Court found the eyewitness accounts reliable and the medical report deficient and in conflict with the other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The medical report did not displace the credible eyewitness evidence, and the Court was entitled to rely on the eyewitness account.
issues.legal_principle: Under Kamaljit Singh v. State of Punjab, 2004 Cri LJ 28, minor variations between medical and ocular evidence do not displace the latter unless the medical evidence completely rules out the manner of injury described by eyewitnesses. Madan Gopal Kakad v. Naval Dubey (1992) 3 SCC 204 establishes that expert opinion assists the court but does not bind it; the court must assess the expert’s reasons and the other evidence. A serious contradiction may undermine the prosecution case, but an unreliable or perfunctory opinion does not automatically outweigh trustworthy eyewitness evidence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and eyewitness_account_credible and medical_opinion_conflicts and medical_opinion_does_not_exclude_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_credible: The court finds the eyewitness account reliable and trustworthy.
predicates.medical_opinion_conflicts: The medical opinion differs from the eyewitness account.
predicates.medical_opinion_does_not_exclude_account: The medical opinion does not conclusively rule out the events described by the eyewitnesses.

issues.definition: When a credible eyewitness account conflicts with medical opinion that does not exclude that account, the court may accept the eyewitness account.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s close relationship to the victim does not, without more, make the witness interested or justify rejecting the testimony.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were the deceased’s son and wife, and both were injured during the occurrence.
Their presence at the scene was natural, and the Court found their statements consistent, reliable, and supported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the witnesses’ relationship to the deceased made their testimony unworthy of belief.
issues.legal_principle: Under Dharnidhar v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010) 7 SCC 759, Jayabalan v. Union Territory of Pondicherry (2010) 1 SCC 199, Ram Bharosey v. State of U.P., AIR 1954 SC 704, Mano Dutt v. State of U.P. (2012) 3 SCALE 219, and Satbir Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2009) 13 SCC 790, related or interested testimony must be assessed carefully but cannot be discarded merely because of the witness’s relationship. The relevant concern is whether the witness is unfairly motivated to falsely implicate the accused and whether the testimony is credible.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and witness_related_to_victim and witness_presence_natural and witness_testimony_credible

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.witness_related_to_victim: A witness is closely related to the victim.
predicates.witness_presence_natural: The witness’s presence at the occurrence is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.witness_testimony_credible: The court finds the witness’s testimony credible.

issues.definition: When a related witness was naturally present and gives credible testimony, the testimony is not rejected solely because of the relationship.

issues.legal_issue: Courts should make reasoned findings on deliberate dereliction and may direct disciplinary action against responsible officials, including officials who have retired.
material_facts: The doctor recorded no injuries or cause of death despite other evidence recording injuries, and the investigating officer failed to account for the viscera and omitted the doctor’s explanation from the record.
The Court found that the officials’ conduct involved deliberate dereliction, irresponsible performance, and a designedly defective investigation prejudicial to the prosecution.
Earlier directions to take action against the officials had not been implemented.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the appropriate authorities to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the doctor and investigating officer, whether or not they remained in service, and held that courts should record specific, reasoned findings about such misconduct and may direct appropriate action.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the duties of fair investigation and fair trial and on the public interest in the administration of justice, referring to State of Punjab v. Ram Singh, Ex-Constable (1992) 4 SCC 54, Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar (1995) 6 SCC 31, Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (2006) 3 SCC 374, National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat (2009) 6 SCC 767, and section 2 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. It held that courts should record reasoned findings on deliberate dereliction, designedly defective investigation, and breaches of professional or investigative duties, and may direct disciplinary or other lawful action even where the official has retired.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the conduct of officials involved in the investigation or evidence is considered.
predicates.court_finds_deliberate_official_derelict: The court makes a reasoned finding that an official deliberately failed to perform a duty or acted in serious breach of professional obligations.
predicates.dereliction_impairs_fair_investigation: The official’s conduct compromises or prejudices the proper investigation or trial.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, when the court finds reasoned evidence of deliberate official dereliction that impairs fair investigation, it may direct disciplinary action.

issues.legal_issue: A group’s intentional, unprovoked, sustained attack with a deadly purpose may establish murder committed in furtherance of common intention rather than culpable homicide punishable under Part II of section 304 of the Indian Penal Code.
material_facts: Several assailants arrived together armed with sticks and attacked the deceased without provocation.
They continued the assault despite intervention by the deceased’s wife and son, whom they also injured, and persisted until the deceased fell and died.
The trial court found that the assailants shared a common intention, and the Supreme Court found the intention to kill apparent from the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the request to substitute an offence under Part II of section 304 for murder and upheld the conviction under sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code and distinguished Part II of section 304. It relied on the circumstances showing a shared intention to kill, including the assailants’ arriving together armed, the absence of provocation, and the continued assault. It also referred to Gudar Dusadh v. State of Bihar, 1972 SCC (Cri) 438, in relation to liability where a lathi blow is directed at a vital part of the body.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and assailants_act_together and assailants_share_intention_to_kill and attack_unprovoked and attack_continues_until_victim_falls

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.assailants_act_together: Several assailants act together in the attack.
predicates.assailants_share_intention_to_kill: The circumstances establish that the assailants shared an intention to kill.
predicates.attack_continues_until_victim_falls: The assailants continue the attack until the victim falls or dies.

issues.definition: When assailants act together with a shared intention to kill, begin an unprovoked attack, and continue it until the victim falls, the murder conviction based on common intention is upheld.
